content: Traumatic hyphema occurs when blood enters the anterior chamber of the eye, the space between the cornea and the iris, as a result of significant ocular trauma. This condition can lead to serious complications, though permanent vision loss is uncommon. Potential complications include elevated intraocular pressure, corneal blood staining, anterior and posterior synechiae, and optic nerve atrophy. Individuals with sickle cell trait or disease are particularly vulnerable to increased intraocular pressure and optic atrophy. Rebleeding after the initial hyphema is associated with a higher likelihood and severity of these complications. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of various medical interventions in managing traumatic hyphema. The search for relevant studies included multiple databases and clinical trial registries, with the most recent search conducted on March 22, 2022. The review included randomized and quasi-randomized trials comparing different medical (non-surgical) treatments for traumatic hyphema. There were no restrictions on participant age, gender, trauma severity, or baseline visual acuity. A total of 30 studies, involving 2969 participants, were included in the review. The interventions assessed included systemic and topical antifibrinolytic agents (such as aminocaproic acid, tranexamic acid, and aminomethylbenzoic acid), corticosteroids, cycloplegics, miotics, aspirin, conjugated estrogens, traditional Chinese medicine, monocular versus bilateral patching, head elevation, and bed rest. The findings revealed no evidence that any of these interventions improved visual acuity, whether measured in the short term (within two weeks) or over longer periods. For example, a meta-analysis of two trials showed no significant effect of aminocaproic acid on long-term visual acuity or final visual acuity up to three years after the hyphema. Similarly, oral tranexamic acid showed little to no benefit for visual acuity in four trials. Other interventions also failed to demonstrate statistically significant effects on visual acuity in either the short or long term. Systemic aminocaproic acid was found to reduce the rate of recurrent hemorrhage, as shown in six trials involving 330 participants. However, when two studies that did not use an intention-to-treat analysis were excluded, the strength of this evidence was reduced. Topical aminocaproic acid showed a similar trend in reducing recurrent hemorrhage, but the evidence was of low certainty. Systemic tranexamic acid significantly reduced the rate of secondary hemorrhage in seven trials with 754 participants, and aminomethylbenzoic acid also showed a significant effect in one study. However, the evidence supporting a reduction in complications from secondary hemorrhage, such as corneal blood staining, synechiae, elevated intraocular pressure, or optic atrophy, was limited due to the small number of events. The use of aminocaproic acid was associated with increased adverse effects, including nausea and vomiting, compared to placebo. There was no evidence of a difference in adverse events between systemic and topical aminocaproic acid or between standard and lower drug doses. Systemic aminocaproic acid appeared to prolong the time required for the primary hyphema to resolve, but no other intervention affected this outcome. Evidence on the use of systemic or topical corticosteroids, cycloplegics, or aspirin in traumatic hyphema was limited due to the small number of participants and events in the trials. Similarly, there was no evidence to support differences in outcomes between monocular and binocular patching, or between ambulation and complete bed rest, in terms of the risk of secondary hemorrhage or time to rebleed. In conclusion, there is no evidence that any of the evaluated interventions improve visual acuity in patients with traumatic hyphema. While antifibrinolytic agents such as aminocaproic acid and tranexamic acid may reduce the rate of secondary hemorrhage, systemic aminocaproic acid may delay the resolution of the primary hyphema. The long-term consequences of secondary hemorrhage remain unclear. There is also no strong evidence to support the use of corticosteroids, cycloplegics, or non-drug interventions like patching, bed rest, or head elevation in managing traumatic hyphema. Further research is needed to explore the potential additive effects of combining these interventions.
